description: Grown in India mainly in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, trained on bower or Y-trellis and pruned twice a year in the tropics. Most disease pressure comes after pruning in wet or humid weather.
npk_split: Split between the two prunings: give FYM, P and part of the N right after back (foundation) pruning and the rest of the N with most of the K after forward (fruit) pruning, adjusted by petiole and soil test.

Bacterial leaf spot.name: Bacterial Leaf Spot
Bacterial leaf spot.cause: Xanthomonas citri pv. viticola (Xanthomonas campestris pv. viticola)
Bacterial leaf spot.description: Bacterial disease of leaves, canes and bunch stalks, also called bacterial canker, that flares up in warm rainy weather after pruning. Cankers on canes and bunch stalks reduce yield and carry the disease to the next season.
symptoms: Small dark angular water-soaked spots along the veins, seen first on the leaf underside
Spots turn brown-black with a yellow halo and merge into dead patches
Dark, sunken, cracked cankers on petioles, canes and bunch stalks
Berries stay small and shrivel on cankered bunches
Bacterial leaf spot.spread: Rain splash, wind-driven rain and pruning tools carry the bacteria from cankers on old canes to new leaves.
Bacterial leaf spot.action: Prune out and burn cankered canes in dry weather and spray a copper fungicide right after pruning.

treatment.name: Bordeaux mixture 1%
treatment.dose: 10 g copper sulphate + 10 g lime per litre
treatment.notes: Spray immediately after pruning to protect cut ends.

treatment.name: Copper hydroxide 77 WP
treatment.notes: On new growth at 7-10 day intervals in rainy spells; copper oxychloride 50 WP 3 g/L is an alternative.

treatment.name: Pruning-tool disinfection and dry-weather pruning
treatment.notes: Dip secateurs in disinfectant between vines; do not prune during rain.

Black rot.name: Black Rot
Black rot.description: Fungal disease of leaves and berries favoured by warm, rainy weather. It is of minor importance in India's dry grape regions but can destroy bunches in wet seasons.
symptoms: Round reddish-brown leaf spots with a dark border
Tiny black dots arranged in a ring inside the spots
Berries turn brown, shrivel and become hard black mummies
Dark sunken lesions on young shoots and tendrils
Black rot.spread: Rain splashes spores from mummified berries and infected canes onto young leaves and bunches.
Black rot.action: Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected canes and protect new growth with a fungicide before rain.

treatment.name: Removal of mummified berries and infected canes
treatment.notes: Do this at pruning; mummies left on the vine or ground restart the disease.

treatment.name: Mancozeb 75 WP
treatment.notes: From new shoot growth until berries begin to soften; observe the pre-harvest interval.

Downy mildew.name: Downy Mildew
Downy mildew.description: The most destructive grape disease in India, attacking leaves, shoots, flowers and young bunches in wet or dewy weather. Unprotected vines can lose the whole crop within days after rain.
symptoms: Yellowish, oily-looking patches on the upper leaf surface
White downy growth on the underside below the patches
Patches turn brown and leaves dry and fall
Flower clusters and young berries turn brown and shrivel
Downy mildew.spread: Spores spread by rain splash and wind and infect whenever leaves stay wet from rain or heavy dew.
Downy mildew.action: Spray a protective fungicide before forecast rain and a systemic one as soon as oily spots appear, covering the leaf underside.

treatment.name: Bordeaux mixture 1%
treatment.dose: 10 g copper sulphate + 10 g lime per litre
treatment.notes: Protectant after pruning and before rainy spells.

treatment.name: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP
treatment.notes: At first oily spots; not more than 2 sprays a season to avoid resistance.

treatment.name: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP
treatment.notes: Alternate with the above; observe the pre-harvest interval on the label.

Esca.name: Esca (Black Measles)
Esca.cause: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp. and Fomitiporia spp. (trunk fungi)
Esca.description: A trunk disease in which wood fungi enter through pruning wounds and slowly block the vine's water-conducting tissue. It mostly affects older vines, is uncommon in India, and no spray can cure it.
symptoms: Yellow or red bands between the veins that turn brown, giving a 'tiger-stripe' leaf
Leaf margins dry and scorch
Small dark purple spots on berries
Sudden wilting and drying of a whole arm or vine in hot weather
Dark streaks or soft pale rot inside the trunk when cut across
Esca.spread: Spores released from infected wood in wet weather enter fresh pruning wounds, and infected cuttings carry the disease to new vineyards.
Esca.action: Cut out affected arms or trunks well below the stained wood in dry weather, burn them and seal the cuts.

treatment.name: Trunk renewal
treatment.notes: Saw off below all discoloured wood and retrain a healthy shoot from the base; uproot and burn dead vines.

treatment.name: Bordeaux paste (10%) on pruning cuts
treatment.notes: Apply on large cuts the same day; prune only in dry weather.

treatment.name: Trichoderma paste on fresh pruning wounds
treatment.notes: Protects wounds from new infection; it does not cure infected wood.

Leaf blight.name: Leaf Blight (Isariopsis Leaf Spot)
Leaf blight.description: Late-season fungal leaf spot common in warm, humid weather. Heavy attacks cause early leaf fall, which weakens the canes for the next crop.
symptoms: Irregular or angular dark brown to reddish-brown spots on older leaves
Yellow halo around spots, which later merge into large dead patches
Dark olive-black fungal growth on the underside of the spots
Early yellowing and leaf fall
Leaf blight.spread: Spores from infected and fallen leaves are spread by wind and rain splash.
Leaf blight.action: Collect and destroy fallen leaves and spray a protective fungicide on the remaining foliage.

treatment.name: Mancozeb 75 WP
treatment.notes: Two sprays 10-14 days apart; observe the pre-harvest interval.

treatment.name: Carbendazim 50 WP
treatment.notes: If spots keep increasing; not more than 2 sprays a season.

Powdery mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
Powdery mildew.description: Fungal disease favoured by warm, dry, cloudy weather and shade inside dense canopies. It attacks leaves, canes and berries, causing berry cracking and poor quality.
symptoms: White to ash-grey powdery patches on both leaf surfaces
Leaves curl upward and look dull
Grey powdery coating on berries, which crack or stay small and hard
Dark brown-black blotches on green canes
Powdery mildew.spread: Wind-borne spores spread without rain, and the fungus survives in dormant buds and on canes.
Powdery mildew.action: Spray sulphur or a systemic mildew fungicide at the first sign and remove excess shoots so light and air reach the bunches.

treatment.name: Wettable sulphur 80 WP
treatment.notes: Do not spray in hot weather above 32 °C; it scorches leaves and berries.

treatment.name: Hexaconazole 5 EC
treatment.notes: Not more than 2 sprays a season; long pre-harvest interval, so use before berry softening.

treatment.name: Myclobutanil 10 WP
treatment.notes: Same fungicide group (FRAC 3) as hexaconazole, so do not alternate the two; rotate with sulphur or a different-group fungicide to delay resistance.

healthy.name: Healthy
healthy.description: The leaf shows no sign of disease, pest or deficiency. Keep watching closely after each pruning and during rainy or cloudy spells.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without oily patches, spots or powder
Clean leaf underside with no white growth
Normal shoot and bunch growth
healthy.spread: Not applicable - no disease or pest detected.
healthy.action: Continue canopy management, balanced nutrition and scouting twice a week in wet weather.
